content: Licorice, also spelled liquorice, is derived from the root of the plant Glycyrrhiza glabra. This plant is a legume, related to beans and peas, and is native to southern Europe and parts of Asia. It is a herbaceous perennial that grows up to 1 meter in height, with pinnate leaves measuring approximately 7–15 centimeters in length, consisting of 9–17 leaflets. The plant produces flowers that are 2 centimeters long, ranging in color from purple to pale whitish-blue, arranged in loose inflorescences. Its fruit is an oblong pod, about 2–3 centimeters long, containing several seeds. Cultivation and Uses Licorice thrives in deep, fertile, well-drained soils with full sun exposure. It is typically harvested in the autumn, two to three years after planting. Licorice extract is obtained by boiling the root and evaporating most of the water. The term licorice originates from the Ancient Greek words meaning sweet root. The extract is available in both solid and syrup forms. Its active compound, glycyrrhizin, is a natural sweetener that is over 50 times sweeter than sucrose and exhibits pharmacological effects. The species Glycyrrhiza uralensis contains a higher concentration of glycyrrhizin. Culinary Use Licorice flavor is widely used in various candies. In the United Kingdom, licorice allsorts are particularly popular, while in continental Europe, stronger and saltier licorice candies are preferred. Many licorice candies enhance their flavor with aniseed oil, and the actual licorice content is often minimal. In Yorkshire, England, licorice mixed with sugar was first used as a sweet treat, a practice that continues today. In the Netherlands, licorice candy, known as drop, is a popular confection, with some varieties mixed with mint, menthol, laurel, or ammonium chloride to create salty licorice. Licorice is also used in soft drinks like root beer and in herbal teas, where it imparts a sweet aftertaste. Additionally, licorice flavor is commonly used in medicines to mask unpleasant tastes. In Italy and Spain, licorice is consumed in its natural form, with the root being dug up, washed, and chewed as a mouth freshener. In Italy, unsweetened licorice is often consumed as small black pieces made from 100% pure licorice extract, which has a bitter and intense taste. In Calabria, a popular liqueur is made from pure licorice extract. In Syria, licorice is sold as a drink, and dried licorice root is chewed as a sweet. According to the USDA Food Database, black licorice contains approximately 100 calories per ounce (28 grams). In Chinese cuisine, licorice is used as a culinary spice for savory dishes, often to flavor broths and foods simmered in soy sauce. Similar flavors can be found in anise, star anise, tarragon, and fennel. In Egypt, licorice is the main ingredient in a well-known soft drink called عرقسوس ('erk-soos'). Medicinal Use Powdered licorice root has been used as an effective expectorant since ancient times, particularly in Ayurvedic medicine, where it is also used in tooth powders. Modern cough syrups frequently include licorice extract as an ingredient. Licorice may also be beneficial in treating mouth ulcers and peptic ulcers. Non-prescription treatments for aphthous ulcers, such as Canker Melts, incorporate glycyrrhiza in dissolvable adhesive troches. Licorice is a mild laxative and can be used as a topical antiviral agent for conditions like shingles, ophthalmic herpes, oral herpes, and genital herpes. Licorice affects the endocrine system due to its isoflavones, which are phytoestrogens. It can lower serum testosterone levels, although its effect on free testosterone levels remains unclear. Large doses of glycyrrhizinic acid and glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice extract can lead to hypokalemia and significant increases in blood pressure, a condition known as apparent mineralocorticoid excess. These side effects occur due to the inhibition of the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, which normally inactivates cortisol in the kidneys. This inhibition causes cortisol levels to appear elevated, mimicking the effects of aldosterone excess, even though aldosterone levels remain low or normal. To mitigate these risks, deglycyrrhizinated licorice preparations are available. Licorice also inhibits Helicobacter pylori and is used to aid in the healing of stomach and duodenal ulcers. In moderate amounts, it may soothe an upset stomach. It can be used to treat ileitis, leaky gut syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, and Crohn's disease due to its antispasmodic effects on the bowels. Licorice is considered an adaptogen, helping to regulate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. It is also used for autoimmune conditions such as lupus, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis, and animal dander allergies. In traditional Chinese medicine, licorice is commonly included in herbal formulas to harmonize the other ingredients and to carry the formula into all 12 regular meridians. It is also used to relieve spasmodic coughs. In traditional American herbalism, licorice is a component of the Hoxsey anti-cancer formula. Toxicity Excessive consumption of licorice or licorice candy can be toxic to the liver and may cause hypokalemia, hypertension, and edema. Rare cases of increased blood pressure have been reported with excessive consumption of licorice tea, but these effects are reversible upon discontinuation of the herb. Most cases of hypertension from licorice are due to the consumption of concentrated licorice candy. Doses as low as 50 grams daily for two weeks can cause a significant rise in blood pressure.
